_comment: LIVENESS CLASSIFICATION — what it means for a host to be 'live', decided by READING THE PAGE, never by the HTTP status code alone. The status code answers 'did the server reply', which is a different question from 'is this domain serving the operator's content'. Four failure modes motivate every list below, and each one silently corrupts a case: (1) a parking page, a server default page and a hosting 'account suspended' notice all return HTTP 200, so a status-only check calls them LIVE and the analyst collects pivots off a template shared by millions of unrelated domains; (2) a 404 or 403 returns non-200, so a status-only check calls the DOMAIN dead when only that PATH is gone — the host is registered, resolving and can be re-pointed tomorrow; (3) a Cloudflare interstitial is a bot wall, not a verdict about the target at all, and must classify as UNKNOWN, never dead; (4) an operator parks a domain between campaigns, so 'parked' is the single most REUSABLE state there is and belongs on a watchlist rather than in the discard pile. Every state whose `reuse_watch` is true means: this name is still under the operator's control and can be flipped to live content later — keep collecting it. ADD a marker when you see a template misclassified; the risky direction is REMOVING one, because that turns a boilerplate page back into a 'live' site and manufactures pivots off shared infrastructure.

parking_markers._comment: Lowercased substrings found in the BODY or TITLE of a domain-parking / for-sale / registrar-holding page. These pages return HTTP 200 with a full HTML document, which is exactly why a status-code check cannot see them. A parked domain is REGISTERED, RESOLVING and under someone's control — it is a lead, not a dead end, so this state sets reuse_watch. Matched case-insensitively as a plain substring against the first `marker_scan_chars` of the decoded body.
values: the domain name is for sale
checking if you own this domain
this webpage was generated by the domain owner
this site is not yet configured

parking_nameservers._comment: Nameserver hostname SUFFIXES that belong to domain-parking / monetisation / for-sale platforms. Independent corroboration of the body markers: an operator who parks a name usually delegates it to one of these, and the NS survives even when the parking HTML fails to fetch. Matched as a case-insensitive suffix against each nameserver, trailing dot stripped. NOTE these are PARKING nameservers, not managed-DNS providers — a shared Cloudflare/Route53 NS is ordinary hosting and is handled by the registrant/DNS noise filters, not here.

soft_404_markers._comment: Lowercased substrings of a NOT-FOUND page that the server returns with HTTP 200 — the 'soft 404'. This is the mirror image of the parking problem: the status says success, the content says the resource is gone. It matters for the URL-PATH layer especially, where a campaign kit directory is removed but the host keeps answering 200 for every path. A soft 404 means the HOST is alive and the PATH is dead, so reuse_watch is set: the operator can restore the kit at the same URL.
values: the requested url was not found

suspended_markers._comment: Lowercased substrings of a HOSTING-SIDE takedown or expiry notice. Distinct from parked (the registrar/owner is monetising) and from not-found (the path is gone): here the provider has switched the account off, usually after an abuse report or non-payment. Highly relevant to fraud casework — it dates a takedown, and the operator commonly rebuilds on a new provider within days while KEEPING the domain, so reuse_watch is set.

default_page_markers._comment: Lowercased substrings of a WEB-SERVER DEFAULT page — the stock document a freshly-provisioned nginx/Apache/IIS/Node host serves before any content is deployed. Returns HTTP 200, so a status-only check calls it live. For fraud infrastructure this is one of the most valuable states in the whole vocabulary: it means a server EXISTS and is reachable but the kit has not been uploaded yet, i.e. you are looking at infrastructure ahead of the campaign. reuse_watch is set and should be read as 'check this again soon'.
values: welcome to your new web server
if you see this page, the nginx web server
this is the default welcome page

blocked_markers._comment: Lowercased substrings of a BOT WALL or WAF interstitial. CRITICAL SEMANTICS: a hit here is NOT a verdict about the target — it means the collection FAILED and the page behind it was never seen. It must classify as `blocked` with live=null (unknown), never as dead and never as live. This is the same discipline as the keyless-capability disclosure: a search we were not allowed to run is absence of RECORD, not evidence of absence. Re-collect with --solve-cf, a rendered browser or a residential proxy before drawing any conclusion.
values: enable javascript and cookies to continue

thresholds._comment: Numeric knobs for the content read. `body_read_bytes` bounds how much of the response is downloaded (a liveness check must never pull a whole video). `marker_scan_chars` bounds how far into the decoded body the substring lists are scanned — markers live near the top of a template. `thin_body_chars` is the raw HTML size at or below which a 200 response is treated as content-free rather than live. `min_text_chars` is the visible-text length (tags/script/style stripped) at or below which a 200 response classifies as `empty`: a redirector or a JS-only stub has plenty of HTML but says nothing, and collecting pivots from it produces framework noise. `http_timeout` is the per-request timeout in seconds.

states._comment: THE VERDICT VOCABULARY. One entry per state the classifier can return. `live` is the tri-state answer to 'is this serving the operator's content': true / false / null where null means WE DO NOT KNOW and must say so. `reuse_watch` true means the name is still under someone's control and can be re-pointed to live content later — those hosts belong on a re-check list, not in the discard pile, which is the whole reason a parked domain is worth recording. `dead` true is reserved for states that genuinely evidence the name is gone; note that NO state derived from an HTTP status code alone sets it — only DNS non-resolution does. `note` is what an analyst should do about it.

live.note: Serves real content. Collect pivots normally.

parked.note: Registrar/monetisation holding page. REGISTERED AND CONTROLLED — re-check later; do NOT cluster on the parking template's favicon, analytics or DOM, which are shared by millions of unrelated domains.

default_page.note: Web-server stock page: the host exists, the kit is not deployed yet. Infrastructure ahead of the campaign — re-check soon and pivot on the IP/ASN/TLS rather than the page.

suspended.note: Provider-side suspension or expiry notice. Dates a takedown; the operator usually keeps the domain and rebuilds elsewhere — re-check and pivot on the registrant.

soft_404.note: HTTP 200 but the body says not-found. The HOST is alive and the PATH is gone; the kit can be restored at the same URL.

not_found.note: Hard 404/410 for this path. NOT a dead domain — the server answered. Try the bare root and the Wayback/urlscan path history.

forbidden.note: 401/403. The server is up and refusing US; content unknown. Often an operator's allowlist, a geo-fence or a cloaking rule — try the click-keyed view (--cloak-probe) and a different egress before concluding anything.

blocked.note: Bot wall / WAF interstitial. THE PAGE WAS NEVER SEEN. Absence of record, not evidence of absence — re-collect with --solve-cf, --render or a residential proxy.

empty.note: 200 with no meaningful text (JS-only stub, redirector, blank). May be a client-side-rendered kit — re-collect with --render before judging.

redirected_offsite.note: Redirects to a DIFFERENT registrable domain. The destination is the lead; this name is a doorway the operator still controls.

server_error.note: 5xx. The host answered, the application is broken. Transient — re-check before recording anything.

no_http.note: DNS resolves but no HTTP/HTTPS response (connection refused / timeout / TLS failure). The name is registered and pointed somewhere — this is NOT a dead domain.

unresolved.note: NXDOMAIN — no DNS. The only state that evidences the name is genuinely gone. Even here, check WHOIS: an unexpired domain with no DNS is dormant, not dead, and can be re-pointed.

unknown.note: The check could not reach a conclusion. Report it as unknown; never round it to dead.

policy._comment: The guardrail proper — the rules the classifier enforces so a verdict cannot be produced from thin evidence. `require_content_for_live`: a `live` verdict requires that a response BODY was actually read and passed the marker/thin-content tests; a 200 with no body read can never be reported as live. `never_dead_from_status`: no HTTP status code, on its own, may produce a dead verdict — only DNS non-resolution does, which is what stops a 404 or a 403 from deleting a live domain from a case. `never_dead_when_blocked`: a bot-wall hit forces live=null. `confident` is false whenever the verdict rests on fewer than `min_signals` independent signals (status, content markers, visible-text volume, DNS, nameservers), so a downstream report can hedge instead of asserting.
